domain: AI automation and compliance services for regulated industries

standingAnswers.whatChanged: Three regulatory calendars moved from 'future' to 'this year' since the last cycle. (1) NAIC's Model Bulletin on insurer AI use is now adopted or substantially matched in ~25 states as of the March 2026 NAIC Issue Brief, with a 12-state pilot of the AI Systems Evaluation Tool feeding into planned Fall 2026 National Meeting adoption — examiners are about to start asking for documentation, not just policy language [fact][content.naic.org, 2026-03]. (2) FDA issued its first-ever AI credibility guidance for drug/biologic submissions (Jan 6, 2025) and then, with EMA, ten joint 'Guiding Principles of Good AI Practice' in Jan 2026 — nonbinding but signaling convergence toward a documented standard [fact][fda.gov]. (3) NIH folded AI-use scrutiny directly into standard research-misconduct and grant-compliance review via a May 14, 2026 notice, arriving in the same year OCR is running active HIPAA audits and a Security Rule overhaul is pending. None of this is enforcement yet — consistent with my 12-24 month lag bias, the actual audit findings and penalties are still ahead of us, probably 2027. What's different is that the paperwork obligation (governance files, credibility dossiers, subprocessor documentation) is now due before the enforcement is.
standingAnswers.demandOutpacingSupply: The gap isn't at the top of the market — the top-20 insurers, Big Pharma, and academic medical centers already have compliance headcount and are Deloitte/EY/PwC accounts. It's one tier down: regional/mid-size carriers, mid-cap biotechs, multi-site (not mega) medical groups, and non-flagship research universities that face the identical documentation bar (same NAIC bulletin, same FDA guidance, same NIH notice) with a fraction of the internal compliance staff and none of the Big-4 relationship. This is inference from segment logic, not a measured demand signal — I found no market-sizing source that meets the citation bar, so treat it as a hypothesis to test with outreach, not a fact [inference][confidence 3].
standingAnswers.singleMoveIdWouldMake: Build the NAIC Model-Bulletin governance-file template first (candidate naic-governance-file-regional-insurers below) and take it to three named New England regional/mutual insurers before touching anything pharma-side. It's the highest edgeFit-plus-timing combination, it's buildable from a single public PDF with zero capital, and MassMutual's regime is the one Nick has lived inside most recently and can speak to with specifics an outside generalist can't fake.

candidate.thesis: A mid-size research university's sponsored-programs office will pay for an outside AI-integrity pre-audit of its effort-reporting and grant-compliance file, because NIH's 2026 guidance folds AI-use scrutiny into standard audits and a single bad certification chain can produce six-figure questioned costs.

catalyst.whyNow: NIH published guidance on May 14, 2026 explicitly addressing AI-use integrity concerns (fabrication, falsification, plagiarism risk) in NIH-supported research, placing AI-use review inside standard institutional compliance audits [fact][grants.nih.gov, 2026-05-14][confidence 5]. Separately, federal effort-reporting obligations under 2 CFR 200.430 are a well-documented, longstanding audit-risk area — one cited case involved $218,000 in questioned costs from unverified effort certifications at a single university [fact, secondary-reported][confidence 3 — original audit finding not independently located; treat the dollar figure as reported, not primary-sourced].
catalyst.whatClosesTheWindow: Once universities build the AI-use disclosure step into their existing effort-certification software (many already use systems like Huron/PeopleSoft), the manual review gap this fills closes — likely an 18-24 month window.

candidate.whyNick: This is literally Nick's current-day compliance domain at Harvard (grant compliance, effort reporting, IRB) applied to a different institution — do not target Harvard itself given active employment and outside-activity clearance was scoped to non-competing engagements.
candidate.ethicalNote: Pitched as a pre-audit review, not a headcount-reduction tool — but an automated effort-reporting monitor is exactly the kind of manual-process automation the operator's open question is about. risks.mitigation: Do not compete head-on as a generic 'compliance consultant.' Position narrowly as a low-cost, fast, non-audit-of-record diagnostic/checklist that de-risks before the institution's existing auditor or Huron-type vendor gets involved — a triage product, not a competing audit.

risks.risk: The regulatory urgency the thesis leans on is softer than framed: the May 2026 NIH notice creates program-level enforcement discretion, but no evidence was found that it has (yet) been written into the OMB Compliance Supplement that drives mandatory Single Audit testing — so sponsored-programs offices may not feel a hard, budgeted deadline to buy a pre-audit.
risks.mitigation: Validate directly on discovery calls whether compliance officers perceive this as urgent/budgeted, rather than assuming it from the notice's existence.

risks.mitigation: Replace with the directly-sourced HHS OIG findings (e.g., the Yale case) in any pitch material, and cite NIH's own notice rather than secondary dollar figures.

risks.risk: The niche is already occupied. Established CSV/CSA consulting firms with existing CDMO/biotech account relationships (ProPharma, Freyr) and purpose-built software (CIMCON AIValidator, ValGenesis iVal) already market directly against this exact pain point — a solo new entrant with no brand and 15-30 hrs/week has a structural disadvantage on trust and delivery capacity for a consequential compliance deliverable.
risks.mitigation: Position narrowly as execution/documentation labor a Director can drop into an existing budget line quickly, not as a competing framework or platform — undercut on speed and personal attention rather than compete on comprehensiveness.

risks.risk: The specific buyer scenario in the thesis (a mid-size CDMO/biotech that has ALREADY adopted a commercial AI-assisted deviation/batch-record tool and now needs outside Part-11 validation docs for it) has zero confirmed real-world instances in available sources — the only real enforcement event (Purolea) is a different scenario (small manufacturer misusing AI directly, no formal tool, no CDMO). Demand may not exist yet at the scale or in the form assumed.
risks.mitigation: Test demand directly via ISPE conversations before building any package — treat as an open hypothesis, not a fact, per the candidate brief's own confidence-3 flag.

risks.risk: Nick's Merck-era GxP/Part 11 validation experience is real but predates the January 2025 FDA AI-model-credibility framework by potentially years — the specific skill this thesis monetizes (AI model validation, not classical CSV) is newer than the edge itself, and it's unverified from outside whether Nick's lived experience actually covered model-based/statistical validation versus conventional deterministic software validation.
risks.mitigation: Be explicit in early conversations about which parts of the framework Nick can speak to from direct experience (Part 11 records/signatures, audit readiness, QU sign-off processes) versus which parts (AI model credibility assessment specifically) are new territory being learned in real time.

risks.risk: Liability/insurance exposure: signing off on validation documentation that FDA later finds deficient for a GxP-adjacent AI tool is consequential (per the Purolea precedent, FDA is now actively scrutinizing this exact intersection). Mid-size biotechs may require E&O/professional liability insurance or indemnification from an outside validation consultant that a $500-capital solo operation cannot provide.
risks.mitigation: Scope initial engagements as advisory/gap-assessment work (not final sign-off authority) until liability structure (LLC, insurance) is in place; confirm insurance requirements during first ISPE conversations before quoting any engagement.
